thesis: This episode argues that high-quality, mispriced businesses can be identified by meeting management and assessing 'hair' (issues), while avoiding sectors with structural problems like traditional auto manufacturing. The speaker highlights specific investments in Turkish warehouse operators and energy companies (Occidental, Chevron) that generate strong cash flows for buybacks and dividends, contrasting them with 'CD' (cash cow) status and avoiding speculative drilling.

claims.claim: The speaker found Reesas to be an extremely high-quality, mispriced business with no 'hair' (issues) after meeting the father and son who ran it.
claims.quote: And this time, I could find no hair on it. I could find nothing wrong with it. The father and son who ran it, they seemed like really high-quality people. It just, none of it made any sense.

claims.claim: The speaker bought into Dajas, a warehouse operator in Turkey, which was extremely mispriced and high-quality.
claims.quote: And I ended up in one case with an extremely high-quality business, which was just extremely extremely mispriced. So we bought into this operator of warehouses. It's a Dajas warehouse operator in Turkey.

claims.claim: The speaker decided not to invest in Halk Bank because of 'too much hair' regarding the CFO's imprisonment and sanctions violations.
claims.quote: And so I told my friend after that meeting that, I can deal with hair, but not so much hair. This is too much. Can we just take it down one or two levels? Let's not do the point one and point two peas.

claims.claim: The speaker views Occidental as a 'CD' with no speculative drilling, generating huge cash flows for buybacks and dividends, which Buffett loves.
claims.quote: And so Oxy basically has no, almost no speculative drilling going on. And so, in effect, it looks like a CD. And they're clipping the coupons. And what Oxy is doing is doing is they have a huge gusher of cash flows coming out.

claims.claim: The speaker believes the investment in Chevron is based on non-exploration risk and that Oxy wouldn't have gone to Chevron if it was large enough.
claims.quote: And then they made an investment in Chevron. I think the reason they made the investment in Chevron is also Chevron has a very large position in the Permian Basin. And if Oxy was large enough, they wouldn't have gone to Chevron.

claims.claim: Buffett viewed Occidental as 'U.S. treasuries on steroids' because he doesn't want downside and looked at it as a coupon clipping bet.
claims.quote: And he doesn't want downside. So he looked at Oxy as U.S. treasuries on steroids. And I think that's why he went with that bet. So other questions?

claims.claim: The speaker considers the auto business terrible, citing high capex, unions, finicky customer tastes, and calcified management, calling it one of the larger mistakes he made.
claims.quote: I had made an investment in 2012, and I think this is one of the larger mistakes I made, just because I should have held on, and I didn't hold on long enough. So in 2012, I invested in Fiat Chrysler automobiles, you know. I always hated the auto business. The auto business just badly sucks.
